title: The Narayaniya of the Mahabharata
author: vyasa
attributionNote: The Nārāyaṇīya stands inside the Mahabharata's book of instruction (parvan 12, chapters 321–339), narrated to Arjuna on the field by Bhishma; it is part of the epic's didactic layer and is read in the Pāñcarātra tradition as one of its earliest authorities. GRETIL's e-text was input by Peter Schreiner.
description: The Nārāyaṇīya teaches the worship of Nārāyaṇa as the origin and the end of all things: the seers ask how a man may reach the highest good, and the answer is the doctrine of the single god who pervades the worlds, the four conditions of the devotee, the rite of the twelve-day sacrifice, the thousand names of Vishnu and the dedication of every act to him. It is the point in the epic where Krishna is not only the counsellor of the Pandavas but the god whose knowledge the epic's teaching serves.
historicalContext: Quoted and commented on in the Vedanta and Pāñcarātra literature — Rāmānuja cites it as scripture in his Vedārthasaṃgraha — the Nārāyaṇīya is where the epic and the devotional theology of the temple traditions meet; its verses are invoked in ritual and its recitation counted as merit.
availabilityNote: Complete: the twenty chapters of the Nārāyaṇīya (Mahābhārata 12.321–339), 1,217 verses, streamed from GRETIL at read time. Each passage is one verse, addressed by the epic's own reference (parvan 12, adhyāya 321, verse 1), so the numbering is the one every Mahabharata edition and concordance uses.
